newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia's TRI loses favour on negative talks.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia's TRI loses favour on negative talks.

text.p: The stock of Malaysia's Technology Resources Industries Bhd (TRI) is losing favour among some investors on continued speculation of management woes and stiff competition, telecommunications analysts said.
Once a must-have stock, negative sentiment has plagued Malaysia's largest cellular phone operator in recent weeks.
"I think most people are still sceptical about TRI," said a telecommunications analyst at a foreign brokerage. "The whole industry is fairly negative."
TRI's stock on Friday closed at 5.35 ringgit, almost half of its 12-month high price of 9.45 ringgit. Its year low of 4.50 ringgit was reached on December 17.
"Even at 5.00 ringgit I would still call a 'sell' on the stock," said a broker at a foreign equities house.
TRI officials declined comment to questions sent by Reuters.
Analysts and fund managers said poor sentiment on TRI began with the August 1996 resignation of Rosli Man, president of Cellular Communications Network (M) Sdn Bhd (Celcom).
Celcom is a wholly-owned subsidiary of TRI, and runs the analogue ART 900 and digital Celcom GSM mobile services.
Ramlan Ahmad, senior manager at fund managers Commerce MGI Sdn Bhd in Kuala Lumpur, said Celcom lost market share because it failed to market its services as effectively as its rivals.

Seven operators provide mobile cellular telecommunications services in Malaysia. Arguably, Celcom's biggest rival is Binariang, whose Maxis digital system has attracted more than 100,000 subscribers within its first year of operations, according to Ramlan.
Celcom, operating for eight years, has Malaysia's largest cellular subscriber base of around 900,000.
"Celcom's (digital) GSM service has only been marginally successful," said Ramlan. "A lot of Celcom subscribers have switched to Binariang or the other digital operators."

Binariang, which owns Malaysia's only two telecommunications satellites, is controlled by local Indian tycoon T. Ananda Krishnan. Ananda is rumoured to be eyeing a stake either in Celcom or Malaysian Airline System Bhd (MAS).
Tajudin Ramli, an ethnic Malay businessman, is the chairman of TRI and also of MAS.
Ramlan said of the two targets, Ananda would most likely look at Celcom "due to political reasons".
A source within TRI told Reuters he estimated the number of vice presidents and senior vice presidents who had left the company within the past few months to be "less than 10".
He said two or three had joined Rosli Man, responsible for building up Celcom's operations, when he left for Syarikat Telefon Wireless Sdn Bhd (STW).
Some analysts also said Celcom's management has suffered because Tajudin was too busy elsewhere.
"Malaysian Airlines alone is a major workload, and it is highly cyclical, even more so than the telecommunications industry," said Ramlan.
But not all are bearish on the company.

"The existing management team is competent in running the company, despite losing several key personnel over the last six months," said equities research house Mohaiyani Securities in a recent report.
Industry sources say Celcom's day-to-day operations are now overseen by executive group vice president Wan Aishah Wan Hamid.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-201 4813)
